B. Very Short Answer Questions

Q27. A simple machine is a device that enables us to do work more easily — it allows us to overcome a large resistive force (load) by applying a smaller effort, or to change the direction of effort, or to gain speed.

Official Answer

Q28. For an ideal machine, Work output = Work input, i.e., the machine has 100% efficiency. Load × displacement of load = Effort × displacement of effort.

Official Answer

Q29. M.A. = η × V.R. (or equivalently η = M.A. / V.R.)

Official Answer

Q30. (a) Force multiplier: VR > 1, i.e., effort arm > load arm (MA > 1). (b) Speed multiplier: VR < 1, i.e., effort arm < load arm (MA < 1). A machine cannot be both simultaneously.

Official Answer

Q31. (a) Door — Class II lever (hinge = fulcrum, load near hinge, effort at handle end). (b) Catapult — Class I lever (fulcrum between load and effort). (c) Wheelbarrow — Class II lever (wheel = fulcrum, load between wheel and handles). (d) Fishing rod — Class III lever (effort between fulcrum and load at tip).

Official Answer

Q32. (a) Nodding head — Class I lever (spine/neck joint is fulcrum, neck muscles provide effort at back, weight of head is load at front). (b) Lifting body on toes — Class II lever (toes = fulcrum, body weight = load between fulcrum and heel, calf muscle effort at heel end).

Official Answer

Q33. greater than — in a Class II lever the effort arm is always longer than the load arm, so MA = effort arm/load arm > 1 always.

Official Answer

Q34. Class II lever always has MA > 1. Reason: In a Class II lever, the load is between the fulcrum and the effort. Therefore, the effort arm is always longer than the load arm, making MA = effort arm/load arm > 1.

Official Answer

Q35. Single movable pulley — when the effort moves a distance d upward, the load moves only d/2 upward (VR = 2), so their displacements are different.

Official Answer

Q36. A single movable pulley acts as a force multiplier: MA = 2 (ideal), so only half the load needs to be applied as effort. A single fixed pulley has MA = 1 and gives no mechanical advantage.

Official Answer

Q37. less than — VR = displacement of effort / displacement of load; if displacement of load > displacement of effort, then VR < 1.

Official Answer

Q38. more than (greater than) — ideal MA of a single movable pulley = VR = 2, which is greater than 1.

Official Answer

Q39. speed — scissors are Class I levers; the blades are longer than the handles, so the effort arm < load arm, giving MA < 1 but VR < 1, acting as a speed multiplier.

Official Answer

Q40. 2 — the two segments of rope that support the movable block mean that when effort moves d, the load moves d/2; VR = effort displacement / load displacement = d/(d/2) = 2.

Official Answer

Q41. A lever works on the principle of moments: at equilibrium, the anticlockwise moment of the load about the fulcrum equals the clockwise moment of the effort about the fulcrum. (Load × load arm = Effort × effort arm)

Official Answer

Q42. Greater than — in a Class II lever, load is between the fulcrum and the effort, so the effort arm (distance from fulcrum to effort) is always greater than the load arm (distance from fulcrum to load). Hence effort arm : load arm > 1.

Official Answer

C. Short Answer Questions

Q43. (a) Mechanical Advantage (MA): The ratio of the load (output force) to the effort (input force) applied to a machine. MA = Load / Effort. It has no unit (dimensionless ratio of forces).
(b) Velocity Ratio (VR): The ratio of the displacement of the effort to the displacement of the load in the same time interval. VR = displacement of effort / displacement of load. It has no unit (dimensionless).

Official Answer

Q44. Efficiency (η) is the ratio of the useful work output to the total work input: η = Work output / Work input × 100%.
In a practical machine, efficiency < 100% because: (i) energy is lost against friction in moving parts, and (ii) some energy is used to move the parts of the machine itself (e.g., the movable block in a pulley system). As a result, MA < VR and η < 1.

Official Answer

Q45. Let L = load, E = effort, d_L = displacement of load, d_E = displacement of effort.
Work output = L × d_L
Work input = E × d_E
Efficiency η = Work output / Work input = (L × d_L) / (E × d_E)
Now, MA = L/E and VR = d_E/d_L
So: η = (L/E) × (d_L/d_E) = MA × (1/VR)
Therefore: η = MA/VR, which gives M.A. = η × V.R.

Official Answer

Q46. Class I lever:
1. Fulcrum is between load and effort.
2. MA can be greater than, equal to, or less than 1.
3. Examples: seesaw, scissors, crowbar.

Class II lever:
1. Load is between fulcrum and effort.
2. MA is always greater than 1 (it is always a force multiplier).
3. Examples: nutcracker, bottle opener, wheelbarrow.

Official Answer

Q47. In a Class III lever, effort is between the fulcrum and the load. The effort arm is always shorter than the load arm, so MA = effort arm / load arm < 1 always. Despite requiring a larger effort than the load, the load moves a greater distance than the effort — it is a speed multiplier.
Example: Sugar tongs, fire tongs, forearm of the human body.

Official Answer

Q48. A single fixed pulley is used because it changes the direction of the effort applied. Instead of pulling the load upward (which is inconvenient), the operator can pull the rope downward (using body weight), which is more convenient and comfortable. Though MA = 1 and VR = 1, the advantage lies in the convenience of the direction of applied force.

Official Answer

Q49. Scissors for cutting cloth are Class I levers with blades longer than handles, making the load arm (blade) longer than the effort arm (handle). This gives MA < 1 (speed multiplier) but the tips of the blades travel a much larger distance than the hands, allowing a large area of cloth to be cut quickly with a small movement of the hands. Speed is more important than force in cutting light cloth.

Official Answer

Q50. A jack screw (a type of inclined plane / screw) is provided with a long arm to increase the velocity ratio. VR of a screw jack = 2πL/p, where L is the length of the arm and p is the pitch. A longer arm increases L, increasing VR, and for the same efficiency, MA = η × VR also increases, meaning less effort is needed to lift a heavy load (car).

Official Answer

Q51. (a) Class I lever — the fulcrum is the edge of the hammer head resting on the wood, the nail provides the load at one side, and the effort (hand) is at the other side (handle end).
(b) Example of Class I lever with MA > 1: A crowbar used to lift heavy stones (effort arm is much longer than load arm).

Official Answer

Q52. Advantage: A block and tackle system can achieve a much higher VR (and therefore higher MA) than a single movable pulley (VR = 2). By adding more pulleys, VR = number of rope segments, so very heavy loads can be lifted with small effort.

More pulleys in the fixed (upper) block: Extra pulleys are added to the upper block to maintain the correct arrangement of the rope and to allow the effort to be applied in a convenient direction (usually downward) without adding to the movable (lower) block's weight, which would reduce efficiency.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q53. In Case 1, where E1 > E2. In a Class II lever (potato cutter), the load arm = distance of potato from fulcrum (pivot end). When the potato is closer to the effort (hand) end, the load arm is longer relative to the effort arm, so MA is smaller, meaning more effort is needed. Thus E1 > E2 corresponds to the potato being closer to the hand (effort end) in Case 1.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q54. A pair of scissors belongs to Class I lever. The fulcrum (pivot/rivet) is between the effort (applied at the handles) and the load (object being cut at the blades). This is the defining feature of a Class I lever.

Official Answer

Q55. In a combination of one fixed and one movable pulley (VR = 2), the fixed pulley allows the effort to be applied in a convenient downward direction (rather than upward as in a single movable pulley). This makes it easier to apply effort using body weight. The MA is the same as a single movable pulley (≈2 ideal) but the direction of pull is more comfortable.

Official Answer

Q56. All four statements A–D are correct. VR for any pulley system = number of rope segments supporting the load (movable block). Fixed pulley: 1; Single movable: 2; block and tackle with 3 or 4 supporting segments: 3 or 4 respectively.

Official Answer

Q57. Maximum moment: when force is perpendicular to the rod (moment = F × full length of arm). Zero moment: when force is along the rod (line of action passes through the pivot, so perpendicular distance = 0, moment = 0).

Official Answer

Q58. The balance point will be on the steel side (i.e., in the 50–100 cm region, if steel occupies the higher numbers). The steel half is denser and heavier, so its centre of gravity is closer to the steel side. For the ruler to balance, the fulcrum must be positioned so that the torque of both halves is equal — this requires the fulcrum to be closer to the heavier (steel) end, i.e., on the steel side of the centre.

Q71. (i) Identify each from diagram: the one with F between L and E = Class I; L between F and E = Class II; E between F and L = Class III.
(ii) Class II lever gives maximum MA: its effort arm (F to E = full length) is always longer than load arm (F to L = shorter), giving highest MA. For equal length levers, placing load closest to F in a Class II arrangement maximises MA.

Q72. (a) Derivation:
Efficiency η = Work output / Work input = (L × d_L) / (E × d_E)
= (L/E) × (d_L/d_E) = MA × (1/VR)
Therefore: η = MA/VR, i.e., MA = η × VR.

(b) A stapler (Class III lever): effort is between fulcrum and load. Effort arm < load arm, so MA < 1 — it requires more effort than the load. However, the load end (staple point) moves through a much larger distance/speed than the effort point — it is a speed multiplier. Its use is justified because the large displacement at the output allows the staple to be driven through paper quickly, and the force needed is not too large for a human to provide.

Q81. Fulcrum at 40 cm. Weight of scale W = 100 gf acts at 50 cm.
Anticlockwise moments (about 40 cm):
40 gf × (40 − 10) = 40 × 30 = 1200 gf·cm

Clockwise moments:
100 gf × (50 − 40) = 100 × 10 = 1000 gf·cm
200 gf × (95 − 40) = 200 × 55 = 11000 gf·cm
Total clockwise = 12000 gf·cm

Net clockwise moment = 12000 − 1200 = 10800 gf·cm (excess clockwise).
For equilibrium, place weight m at 0 cm:
m × (40 − 0) = 10800 → m = 270 gf.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q82. Let W = weight of scale acting at 50 cm (its centre of mass).
Fulcrum at 70 cm. Moments about 70 cm:
Anticlockwise (left side): 2 N × (70 − 0) = 2 × 70 = 140 N·cm; W × (70 − 50) = 20W N·cm.
Clockwise (right side): 5 N × (100 − 70) = 5 × 30 = 150 N·cm.

Equilibrium: 140 + 20W = 150
20W = 10
W = 0.5 N.

Q83. The scale's weight W acts at its centre of gravity = 50 cm.
Fulcrum at 60 cm. For equilibrium:
Anticlockwise moment = W × (60 − 50) = 10W
Clockwise moment = m × (75 − 60) = 15m

Setting equal: 10W = 15m → W = 1.5m.

Conclusion: The mass (weight) of the scale is greater than m (specifically 1.5 times m). The fulcrum is to the right of the scale's centre, so the scale overhangs more to the left; to balance, the scale's weight must be greater than m.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q84. Let the balance point be at distance x cm from the 0 cm end.
Scale's weight acts at 50 cm.
For equilibrium, taking moments about the balance point x:
Sum of clockwise = Sum of anticlockwise.
Let fulcrum be at x from 0 end.
Anticlockwise forces (left of x): 200 gf at 0 → moment = 200 × x
Clockwise forces (right of x): 200 gf at 50 cm → moment = 200 × (50 − x) if x < 50, else clockwise term changes sign. 100 gf at 100 cm → moment = 100 × (100 − x).

For x < 50 (likely): 200x = 200(50 − x) + 100(100 − x)
200x = 10000 − 200x + 10000 − 100x
200x = 20000 − 300x
500x = 20000
x = 40 cm.

The scale must be supported at the 40 cm mark.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q85. Balance point C is at 45 cm from A, so AC = 45 cm, CB = 35 cm.
For equilibrium about C, the net moment = 0.

Let weight of AC portion = W₁ (acts at its centre = 22.5 cm from A, i.e., 22.5 cm from C on left).
Let weight of CB portion = W₂ (acts at its centre = 17.5 cm from B, i.e., 17.5 cm from C on right).

Anticlockwise moments: 100 gf × 45 cm + W₁ × 22.5
Clockwise moments: 100 gf × 35 cm + W₂ × 17.5

For uniform rod (uniform density): W₁/W₂ = AC/CB = 45/35 = 9/7.
So the weight of AC section is greater than BC section in ratio 9:7.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)

Q86. (i) The 50–100 cm region weighs more. The balance point (40 cm) is to the left of centre (50 cm), meaning the right half (50–100 cm) is heavier — it needs to be closer to the fulcrum to balance, which means more weight on the right side.

(ii) When supported at 50 cm (centre), we need to find the extra weight.
Let the right half (50–100 cm) have weight W_R and left half (0–50 cm) have weight W_L.
W_L + W_R = 50 gf total.

From original balance at 40 cm:
W_L acts at 25 cm, W_R acts at 75 cm.
Anticlockwise: W_L × (40 − 25) = 15W_L
Clockwise: W_R × (75 − 40) = 35W_R
15W_L = 35W_R → W_L = (7/3)W_R
W_L + W_R = 50 → (7/3)W_R + W_R = 50 → (10/3)W_R = 50 → W_R = 15 gf; W_L = 35 gf.

At 50 cm support:
Anticlockwise: W_L × (50 − 25) = 35 × 25 = 875
Clockwise: W_R × (75 − 50) = 15 × 25 = 375
Net anticlockwise = 875 − 375 = 500 gf·cm (left heavier, tilts left).
Add weight m at 100 cm: m × 50 = 500 → m = 10 gf.

Model Answer (not an official mark scheme)
